name: Face slimming strap
lead: A face slimming strap is an elastic band worn under the chin and over the head or ears to compress the lower face and neck. It is marketed for a tighter-looking jawline and a less prominent double chin, and is sold mainly through online marketplaces and social media. Users typically wear it for a period at home, and some products are designed for wear during sleep. Similar chin straps are also used in medical settings, for example to keep the mouth closed during positive airway pressure therapy [1].

The appearance chain proponents describe is mechanical: upward compression holds the soft tissue under the jaw in a more defined position and may shift fluid for a time, giving a sharper profile while the strap is on. Users often pair straps with jaw exercises, facial massage or mewing-related routines in the same jawline-focused routine.

Published research on straps for appearance is absent from the literature reviewed. Systematic reviews of non-surgical submental treatments cover injectable deoxycholic acid, cryolipolysis, radiofrequency and similar methods and do not include compression straps [2]. A small case report of a commercial jaw exerciser found no change in jawline or double chin [3].

paras: Face slimming straps are typically made of stretchy fabric with a hook-and-loop or adjustable closure. Some versions are described as V-line or sleep straps and are marketed to be worn for hours or overnight. The strap sits under the chin and over the crown or in front of the ears, applying upward pressure.

Wikipedia describes two broad causes of a double chin: excess fat that sags under the chin in some overweight people, and a skeletal pattern in which the jaw bones do not project far forward, so the chin appears to blend into the neck even at low body fat [5]. Which cause applies matters for the treatments discussed below, since a strap acts on soft tissue from outside and does not change bone or fat volume.

The claimed mechanism is external compression of the submental region, which proponents say may temporarily shift fluid or hold the soft tissue in a more defined position. Fat reduction in the neck by established methods works by destroying fat cells chemically or with energy delivered to the tissue, as described in reviews of deoxycholic acid injection and cryolipolysis.[2] A compression band does not use these mechanisms.

Established options for submental fat described in the literature include injectable deoxycholic acid, which destroys fat cells that the body then clears over several months; the US FDA announced approval of it as Kybella for moderate-to-severe fat below the chin in April 2015, and it was produced by Kythera Biopharmaceuticals [6][4]. Other categories include cryolipolysis, radiofrequency and focused ultrasound [2]. Surgical options noted by Wikipedia include hyoid lift, genioplasty and orthognathic surgery [5]. A generic deoxycholic acid injection became available in the US in April 2021 [6]. Wikipedia's article on double chin does not mention compression garments or chin straps [5].
No studies found of compression straps for slimming the face or reducing a double chin.

A 2026 systematic review of 30 studies of nonsurgical treatments for submental fullness covered injectable deoxycholic acid (17 studies), cryolipolysis (11), radiofrequency (3), novel injectables, focused ultrasound, diode laser and a combined device, with liposuction for comparison. A pooled analysis of eight deoxycholic acid studies found a responder proportion of 70.8 percent with high heterogeneity, and adverse events were mostly mild and transient. The review did not include compression garments or straps, and its authors noted that many included studies were open-label or industry-sponsored.[2]
Deoxycholic acid injection (ATX-101) was approved for submental fat in the United States as Kybella and in Canada as Belkyra, and trials reported common injection-site reactions.[4]

A 2024 case report followed two men who used a commercially available silicone jaw exerciser for about three months, one to three times a week. Neither participant showed a change in double chin, jawline or face and neck tightness by before-and-after photographs, and neither was satisfied with the product's feel. Both participants were also authors, no objective measurements were taken, and the authors called for larger studies.[3]

Reported or plausible issues include skin irritation, pressure marks and discomfort, and the possibility that a tight strap interferes with comfortable breathing or sleep. No safety study of cosmetic straps has been published. Medical chin straps used with positive airway pressure have been studied for their effect on treatment compliance, which is a separate application [1].

Straps are discussed alongside jaw exercisers, chewing gum and mewing-related devices as inexpensive options for jawline definition. Advocates say the visual tightening is noticeable while the strap is worn, and users share before-and-after photos taken with and without the band. No published study has measured sustained change, and no looksmaxxing forum material is documented here beyond this general positioning.

timeline.event: A study of chin straps used with positive airway pressure therapy reports on compliance and nightly use [1].
FDA announces approval of deoxycholic acid injection (Kybella) for fat below the chin [6].
Phase III trial reports on patient experience with ATX-101 (Kybella/Belkyra), approved for submental fat [4].
Generic deoxycholic acid injection becomes available in the US [6].
Case report of two men using a commercial jaw exerciser finds no change in double chin or jawline [3].
Systematic review of nonsurgical submental fullness treatments does not include compression straps [2].

angle.text: Users wear the strap to hold the submental area snug, aiming for a more defined jaw and less visible double chin. Sellers describe a visible tightening while it is on.
